# Handwrite

> Handwrite turns a photograph of your own handwriting into an installable
> OpenType font family — Regular, Bold, Italic, Bold Italic — with measured
> spacing, generated kerning, and three variants of every character so repeated
> letters do not look rubber-stamped. It is free, needs no account, and does all
> of its work inside the visitor's browser: no handwriting, photograph or font
> is ever uploaded anywhere.

Site: https://handwritingfont.vercel.app
Source: https://github.com/heistkit/handwriting (MIT)

This file exists because the app is a client-side application: the guide, the
legal documents and the help text are rendered by JavaScript modules, so a
crawler that does not execute them sees the landing page and nothing else.
Everything below is the same information those screens contain, in a form that
does not need a renderer.

## What it does

You copy a printed list of characters onto blank paper in your own hand,
photograph the page, and the app returns a `.zip` containing four `.otf` files,
web font files, and a CSS snippet. The font installs like any other font and
works in any application that can pick a font.

## Requirements

- Any modern browser. A desktop machine is easier for the review step; phones work.
- Blank paper and a pen. A fine-liner or gel pen around 0.5 mm is best.
- A phone camera or a flatbed scanner.
- Nothing else. No account, no sign-up, no payment, no software to install.

## The steps

1. **Write.** Copy the characters onto paper. There are four sheets — everyday
   letters (32 characters: lowercase plus the six commonest punctuation marks),
   capitals (26), numbers and maths (31), and symbols (23), 112 in total. The
   first sheet on its own produces a working, usable font; the rest add coverage.
   A printable sheet with guide boxes is available, printed in a blue that drops
   out during processing so the boxes are never traced into the letters.
2. **Photograph.** Lay the page flat, light it evenly, hold the camera parallel
   to the page. The shot does not need to be square: rotation is corrected and
   lighting is evened out region by region.
3. **Review.** Every character is shown as the app read it. Anything wrong can be
   redrawn by hand in the browser.
4. **Refine.** Type a sample line, adjust spacing and weight, name the family.
5. **Download.** The zip arrives in your downloads folder.

About ten minutes, most of it writing.

## Rules that decide whether it works

- **Do not let characters touch.** This is the one failure the app cannot
  repair — two characters written so their ink connects are read as one shape.
  A gap about one letter wide is plenty.
- **Do not use pencil.** It photographs faint and graphite catches the light, so
  the same stroke reads dark in one place and pale in another.
- **Do not use a broad marker.** Thick strokes merge into blobs.
- **Use one pen throughout.** Switching partway shows up as uneven weight.
- **Write the way you normally write.** Careful block capitals produce a stiff,
  generic font. The slight inconsistency between one letter and the next is what
  makes handwriting look handwritten.

## Installing the font

- **Windows** — extract the zip, select all four `.otf` files, right-click, Install. Restart apps that were already open.
- **macOS** — drag the four `.otf` files into Font Book, or double-click each and press Install Font.
- **Linux** — copy them into `~/.local/share/fonts/`, then run `fc-cache -f -v`.
- **iOS** — cannot install a font from the Files app on its own. A font-installer app from the App Store adds it as a configuration profile, which then has to be approved in Settings. This is an iOS restriction, not something the app can work around.
- **Android** — most apps cannot use a custom font at all. Some launchers and note-taking apps load an `.otf` directly; system-wide installation needs a rooted device. The web font files in the zip are usually more useful here.

## Privacy

Reading the photograph, tracing the letters and building the font all happen in
the browser tab. There is no upload, no account, and no server involved in any
part of the processing. The network is used for one thing: fetching the app's
own code, some of which loads on demand.

The served page carries a content-security policy containing `connect-src
'none'`, which means the browser itself refuses to let the page make any
outbound request at all. That is checkable in any browser's developer tools
rather than something a visitor has to take on trust.

Seven small values are kept in the browser's local storage — theme, text size,
motion preference and similar. No cookies, no session storage, no analytics.

Work in progress is also kept, on the device, so that closing the tab does not
throw away a sheet somebody filled in by hand: the traced outlines of the
characters, which step was reached, and the tuning settings, in the browser's
own IndexedDB. Not the photographs — those are discarded when the tab closes
and are never written to storage. It can be switched off in Settings, and the
same panel erases it on demand. None of it is transmitted; there is no server
to transmit it to.

## Ownership

Fonts made with Handwrite belong entirely to the person who made them. No
licence to follow, no attribution, no restrictions, commercial use included.
The application's own source code is MIT.

## How it works, technically

There is no machine-learning model anywhere in it, and that is a design decision
rather than a limitation. Because the app tells you exactly which characters to
write and in what order, it never has to *recognise* handwriting — it already
knows what each shape is meant to be. It only has to find the ink and read it
left to right, which is classical image processing with no inference step to be
wrong about.

- **Preprocess** — Sauvola local thresholding via summed-area tables, so a shadow across one corner binarises correctly. Rotation corrected by maximising the sharpness of the ink projection profile.
- **Segment** — connected components grouped into characters by merging pieces stacked vertically, which reunites the dot of an `i` with its stem. Because the expected count per row is known, a row that comes up long fuses its closest pair and one that comes up short splits its widest glyph at its narrowest waist.
- **Trace** — contours walked along pixel edges, corners detected on the raw walk before smoothing can hide them, then fitted with cubic Bézier curves.
- **Metrics** — side bearings set from each glyph's own ink profile so the *perceived* gap is even: a flat `H` gets the full bearing, a round `o` less, a diagonal `A` less still. Baselines are recovered from unruled paper by solving ascender and descender constraints across a whole row at once.
- **Compile** — bold synthesised by displacing outline points along their own outward normals, italic by shearing about the middle of the x-height band. Three variants per character rotate through a `calt` chaining substitution. Kerning is written as a class-based GPOS table.

## Common questions

**Is anything I write uploaded?** No. Everything happens in the browser tab.

**Who owns the font?** You do, entirely — including commercial use and resale.

**Why `.otf` and not `.ttf`?** Both are OpenType and install identically. The
`.otf` format carries cubic Bézier outlines, which is exactly what the tracer
produces, so nothing is lost in conversion.

**Do I have to write everything four times for bold and italic?** No. You write
once; the other three styles are generated geometrically from that sample.

**Why do my letters look slightly different each time?** Deliberate. Three
variants of each character rotate as you type. It can be switched off.

**How is spacing decided?** Measured, not guessed — from the ink profile down
each side of every character.
